audio.narration: They called it the Palace of Ten Thousand Words. Each room was a character. Each corridor was a sentence. The entire structure was a living poem — written three thousand years ago by the First Calligrapher. Every soldier carried a character. Every wall told a story. The palace was not built OF words — it was built BY them. Every character was a load-bearing element of the structure. Remove one, and part of the palace would collapse. He traced the thousand characters. Each one reinforced the next. Remove any single word and the palace would buckle. But there — at the very center, largest and oldest — he found the KEY. The character that anchored everything. His mother. The woman who had dipped his finger in blood. Who had made him paint the word that started the war. She was not just his mother. She was the architect of this palace. The First Calligrapher. The one who had written the empire into existence. She had written him too. She had written him into this moment — with the word 'war' — because she knew that the only one who could rewrite her palace was the one she had made to understand its deepest truth. That words, once written, could never truly be erased. Only overwritten.
